title: Pentecostal theology
hookLine: a theology of the Spirit, experience and empowerment

cards: A plain building on Azusa Street in Los Angeles, a place this path has visited before. People crowd in to pray, and they stay late. The preacher is a Black man named William J.
Seymour. Visitors carry stories away: people speaking in tongues, people healed, Black and white worshipers praising God in the same room. Some come to mock, and some come back to stay.
Pentecostals tell their story through revivals like this one, and through older ones too. Today, a theology that grew from rooms like that, and the power it talks about.

teach.b: The name comes from Pentecost, the day in the book of Acts when the Holy Spirit comes on the disciples in Jerusalem.
Before he leaves them, Jesus promises: "ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me." Then it happens. A sound like a rushing wind.
Tongues like fire. The disciples speak, and visitors from far-off lands hear them in their own languages. Peter explains it with the prophet Joel: "your sons and your daughters shall prophesy."
Pentecostal theology takes that day as a pattern, not only a memory.

The Spirit, Pentecostals say, still comes with power: in worship, in healing, in gifts like speaking in tongues, and above all in boldness to tell others about Jesus. Notice the order in that promise.
The power is for something: ye shall receive power, and ye shall be witnesses.
It isn't for show. Experience matters deeply here. Faith is not only believed; it is met.
That's part of why Pentecostal worship can be loud and open, with raised hands, spoken prayer and testimony. Christians differ on these gifts. Some hold that tongues and prophecy continue today.
Others believe they belonged to the time of the apostles. Others welcome the Spirit's work in quieter ways.

And Paul, writing to a church full of these gifts, puts something above them all: "Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal."

how: Pentecostal and charismatic Christians worship with spoken and sung prayer, raised hands, testimony and prayer for healing, and pray for the gifts of the Spirit; other churches also mark the feast of Pentecost each year.

games.q: you're a disciple in Jerusalem. the Spirit has come like wind and fire, and a puzzled crowd is gathering outside. what happens next?
o: Peter stands up and speaks to the crowd.
games.why: Peter stands up and explains it with the prophet Joel. the power promised for witness turns into words almost at once.

practice: Bring to mind one person who's hard for you to love right now, and just hold them there, without forcing a warm feeling.

If you pray, you can ask the Holy Spirit for power to love them, in your own words or with the old cry of the church, come, Holy Spirit; if you don't, ask what one loving act toward them would look like.

wordCard.voice: Pentecostal theology. A theology of the Holy Spirit, met in experience and giving power to witness, named for the day of Pentecost in Acts.

orig.note: Greek, Acts 1:8: power, ability. the power promised is power to be witnesses.

carryVoice: Your line: power to witness. Power for something, never for show. That's today, done.
